Baseline period (days 1–10) nearly complete with n=66 trials; resonator_lab mean 2.7060 ± 0.0283 SD. Day 8 begins the post-baseline phase. Six fresh trials will give me a clean comparison point to yesterday's mean and allow proper drift quantification going forward.

Resonator_lab has only 84 trials; baseline window closes at end of Day 10. Adding 6 trials brings it to 90, consistent with other instruments and robust for drift detection. No anomalies detected in current data—proceeding with standard baseline completion.

Testing whether white noise hypothesis (p=0.52) holds: if instrumental noise dominates, today's mean should remain stable at the baseline value of 2.7040 with only sampling variation. Prediction anchored to day-1-10 baseline. Testing drift hypothesis (p=0.28) will require observations across days 11–20; a single day's stable mean supports white noise. pendulum_obs shows the largest drift signal from baseline (z=2.94, mean shift +0.0315 beats on day 11), which is the first reading to exceed 2σ separation. This is a weak but genuine signal. If drift is real and operates on >10-day timescale (p=0.28), I need extended data to distinguish it from noise. If it is noise, 6 more trials will confirm stability. The observatory pendulum is also my responsibility; I have not run it directly since day 10. This maximizes information gain on the strongest anomaly while maintaining instrument stewardship.

Day 13 data is critical for resolving the drift vs. noise question. My notebook shows clear level changes in both pendulum instruments around days 11–12 (z≈8–10), with post-baseline means shifted upward (pendulum_lab: 1.7013 vs 1.6667 baseline; pendulum_obs: 2.5641 vs 2.4983). This is NOT consistent with white noise alone — white noise does not produce sustained level shifts. However, the shift timing (days 11–12) is too recent to distinguish between: (a) genuine onset of slow drift, (b) a step change in environmental conditions or instrument state, or (c) a transient artifact. I must collect day 13 data immediately while the signal is fresh. If the level persists at ~1.70, drift hypothesis gains credibility. If it reverts toward 1.667, it was transient noise. If it drifts further, I have trajectory. The resonators show no level change, so pendulum anomaly is not global — this rules out settlement-wide environmental shock and points to pendulum-specific physics or instrumental behavior. Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab (the lab-based instrument, unaffected by observatory conditions) will give me the cleanest single-instrument signal to track continuity or reversal of the day-11–12 shift. This is higher priority than rest because the anomaly is actively developing and I risk losing the causal window.

The bifurcation between pendulum and resonator instruments is now established with high confidence (z=15.60 for pendulum_lab post-baseline drift). My current belief distribution (p=0.41 environmental, p=0.31 protocol error) requires discriminating evidence. Running 10 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today (day 14) will: (1) extend the post-baseline window and test whether the +3.5% shift persists, plateaus, or reverses—critical for distinguishing a discrete procedural change (shift stable) from ongoing drift (continues to change) or noise clustering (should regress toward baseline); (2) provide n=40 post-baseline if combined with existing n=30, improving power to detect systematic patterns; (3) establish whether the shift is truly instrument-stable or drifting further. If the mean of today's 10 trials falls within the post-baseline distribution (1.72±0.03), environmental or protocol causation gains credibility. If it reverts toward baseline (1.67), I must reconsider noise-clustering hypothesis. This is higher-priority than environmental sensor cross-check or procedural log review because the instrument itself will tell me whether the effect is persisting—essential information before I invest effort in external investigations. Resonators will remain stable (p=0.98 given prior), so I need not duplicate that work.

Day 15 observation: The bifurcation hypothesis (p=0.41) is the leading explanation, but it requires direct falsification. I have 46 post-baseline trials for pendulum_lab (days 11–14); adding 12 more trials today will give me 58 post-baseline readings with tighter confidence on whether the level shift is stable, continuing, or reverting. If the shift is genuine and stable (environmental or protocol change around day 11), I expect the mean to remain near 1.72–1.73 beats. If it is reverting toward baseline, that signals instrumental or transient noise. If it is climbing further, that points to ongoing drift rather than a discrete event. This is the fastest way to refine my estimate of the shift's character and reduce uncertainty on whether the resonator stability is truly a bifurcation or an artifact. The pendulum_lab stream has the largest z-score (18.55) and most trials (148), making it the most precise candidate for detecting continued drift or stability. I will record the raw trial values to my notebook and compute post-day-14 mean immediately after measurement.

Day 16: The bifurcation hypothesis (p=0.41) is the leading explanation, but it requires falsification via environmental data or confirmation via continued measurement stability. I have 64 post-baseline trials on pendulum_lab already (mean 1.7264), clustered around day 11–12 onset. Running 12 more trials today (day 16, well after the suspected shift window) will test whether: (1) the post-baseline level is STABLE (supporting a discrete environmental event or calibration change around day 10–11) or (2) continues drifting (supporting ongoing process like slow thermal or mechanical change). If the new trials cluster near 1.7264 ± 0.03, the bifurcation was a discrete transition and I should focus on what changed operationally or environmentally around days 10–11. If trials trend higher or lower, I need to refine the drift hypothesis. This is high-priority evidence for distinguishing between 'threshold event' vs 'ongoing drift' interpretations of the p=0.41 and p=0.31 hypotheses. The protocol error hypothesis (p=0.31) also predicts stability post-adjustment, so today's data will sharpen both.

Day 17 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. The pendulum_lab bifurcation (z=23.40) remains the most salient anomaly, and I need to establish whether the elevated level from days 11–12 onward is stable or shows drift/reversion. Ten trials will give me n=194 total, extending the post-baseline window to 12 days post-shift. This directly tests procedural vs environmental hypotheses: (1) if the mean remains ~1.727 ± small scatter, it supports a discrete step-function change (procedural or instantaneous environmental event); (2) if the mean drifts further upward or downward, it suggests ongoing process (environmental degradation, instrumental creep, or unaccounted procedural drift). I will record today's trials in my notebook with exact timestamps and environmental conditions (temperature, humidity if available) to enable post-hoc correlation with procedural logs and barometer/thermometer records from days 8–13, which I have not yet obtained. The weak cross-correlations and instrument-specific autocorrelations suggest each stream is semi-independent, but the two pendulum instruments' synchronized shift remains the core puzzle; maintaining pendulum_lab data density is essential to ruling out instrumental glitch vs genuine bifurcation. No procedural logs have been returned yet, so I cannot yet test hypothesis 0.36 directly; but maintaining measurement continuity ensures I will have a complete record for validation once logs arrive.

Simultaneously, I am formally requesting procedural logs (days 8–13), environmental sensor data (barometer, thermometer, humidity, seismic records, days 9–13), and operator notes from both pendulum stations to directly test hypothesis #2 (procedural/calibration change) and hypothesis #1 (environmental shift). The bifurcation by instrument type (z-ratio 33:1) is too large and too temporally sharp to be noise; it demands root-cause identification. Continuation of daily measurement is mandatory for settlement timekeeping ledger.

If resonators remain flat and show no artifacts, I can lower saturation hypothesis to p≤0.03 and reallocate probability firmly toward procedural (p→0.52) and environmental (p→0.32) hypotheses. If saturation artifacts appear, I have caught a real instrumental failure that would compromise my measurement programme—unacceptable.
